title: Have you forgetten?
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino argues that experienced teachers have forgotten how overwhelming it is to be a trainee. She recalls her own training year of late nights, endless planning and marking, and unfocused reflection, then contrasts it with the comfort she now has after years of support. Friends criticise trainees for being panicky, late with plans or slow to act on advice, and she admits to having thought the same. She draws a parallel with the disrupted remote and hybrid teaching year, when veteran teachers also felt like novices. Her move is to apply to trainees what teachers already do for students: chunk the load, build in retrieval and focus on one thing at a time. The piece is a short, reflective call for empathy in mentoring.
points: Expertise breeds forgetfulness: experienced teachers lose sight of how much a novice must juggle at once.
Common complaints about trainees (panic, late plans, ignored advice) are explained by overload rather than lack of effort.
The pandemic teaching year is offered as a shared memory of novice-style overwhelm that veterans can draw on.
Mentors should treat trainees as they treat students, breaking development into manageable chunks and one focus at a time.
quotes: I think we have forgotten what it is like to be a trainee teacher. When I trained, I remember working late into the night, desperately looking for resources to use,
I remember trying to reflect on different aspects of my lessons but not focusing on the right things. I remember feeling quite lost on some days and overwhelmed on others.

Now I have the privilege of providing actionable feedback to trainees that teach my classes. Watching trainee teachers work hard and focus on improving their practice is inspiring! It makes me consider how I teach, how I position myself in the classroom, the language I use and so much more.
When talking to friends about trainee teachers, sometimes I get the feeling that we may have forgotten how hard it is, to not only balance everything, but to also make small gains.
When you are a novice at something, it can feel overwhelming (and lonely) as circumstances or experts try to develop you too quickly.
It is so important to apply this to trainee teachers too. Focus on one thing at a time, build up good practice, and be mindful about how much our trainee teachers need to accomplish in a year.
